At a hearing held today, Apple is challenging the UK government's refusal to publicly confirm whether it has issued an order demanding the company provide access to users' encrypted data. Details below.

A bit of background

Earlier last year, The Washington Post reported that the UK government had secretly ordered Apple to build a backdoor into all content uploaded by global users to iCloud.

The order itself was also subject to strict secrecy rules, with Apple not even permitted to publicly confirm or discuss the request.

The UK government has long maintained a policy of 'neither confirm nor deny' the existence of individual such orders, and companies bound by them are restricted from disclosing that they have received them.

In response to the reportedly issued but officially unconfirmed order, Apple withdrew the option to enable Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for iCloud users in the UK.

The reason is that when ADP is enabled, iCloud backups and other categories of iCloud data are end-to-end encrypted. Rather than comply with the UK backdoor order, Apple therefore simply stopped offering ADP to new users in the UK entirely, despite the reported order applying to global users.

At this point, Apple and the UK government are facing off on two fronts: both the underlying demand for access to encrypted data, and the secrecy rules preventing Apple from publicly discussing that demand.

In April 2025, a judge rejected the UK government's attempt to keep the details of Apple's legal challenge secret, ruling that disclosing the case's existence would not harm national security.

Months later, under pressure from the White House, the UK government dropped the portion of its secret order seeking access to U.S. users' data. However, the demand did not disappear entirely: the UK subsequently issued a new notice targeting Apple users within the UK.

Fast-forwarding to a few weeks ago, reports indicated that Apple had once again launched a legal challenge against the UK government, as the original order targeting global users had been replaced by a new order specifically targeting UK users.

Which brings us to today.

Apple Challenges Secrecy of the Order

According to Reuters, Apple appeared at a hearing before London's Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) today, challenging the UK government's continued refusal to confirm or deny the existence of a new Technical Capability Notice.

According to Reuters, Apple's lawyers argued that the government's secrecy policy impedes meaningful public discussion of the case and undermines the principle of open justice.

The following is an excerpt from the report:

At Thursday's hearing, Ben Jaffey, a lawyer representing the advocacy groups Privacy International and Liberty, said the government's position had become 'absurd.' He noted that 'the horse has bolted,' meaning the information is already public. He said U.S. politicians and officials have publicly referenced the original notice, while unnamed UK government sources have confirmed the matter to the media. Both he and Apple's lawyers argued that the UK government's 'neither confirm nor deny' (NCND) policy is an affront to open justice and hinders meaningful public discussion of the issue.

It should be clarified that today's hearing focused on the secrecy of the order, not on whether the UK government has legal authority to demand access to Apple's encrypted data.

Following the hearing, the IPT will decide whether the government can continue to apply its 'neither confirm nor deny' policy in this case. According to Reuters, a full hearing on Apple's challenge to the Technical Capability Notice itself is unlikely to take place before next year.
